blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The CIs and p-values of linear regression rest on four assumptions, often remembered as LINE: Linearity, Independence of observations, Normality of residuals, and Equal variance of residuals (homoscedasticity).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Least squares will fit a line to any data (§12.2.2). Whether that line and its standard errors mean what they claim depends on these four conditions. Each protects a different part of the output.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If weight gain slowed in the older children but a straight line were fitted anyway, the line would over-predict at the ends of the age range and under-predict in the middle. The residual plot would show a curve (§12.5.1). For the clinic register the four standard plots show none of the warning patterns: the residuals scatter evenly around zero, follow the Normal line, keep a constant spread, and no child has a large Cook’s distance (a measure of how much one child moves the fitted line, defined in §12.5.2).

blocks.alt: The four standard regression diagnostic plots for weight on age
blocks.caption: Figure 12.3. The four standard diagnostic plots (R’s default set of regression plots) for weight on age in the clinic register. 1: residuals against fitted values, with a smoother, checks linearity. 2: Normal Q-Q plot of standardised residuals (residuals scaled to SD units, §12.5.1) checks normality. 3: Scale-Location, √|standardised residual| against fitted values, checks equal variance. 4: standardised residuals against leverage (how far a child’s age lies from the mean age) check for influential points (§12.5.2). All four look healthy here.

points.html: Linearity protects the coefficient itself. If the true relationship is curved, a straight-line slope describes something that does not exist. Check with the scatter diagram and the residuals-vs-fitted plot; §12.4.5 shows how to model a curve.

Independence protects the standard errors. Repeated measurements on one child, or children sampled within the same village, carry less information than independent observations. The model treats them as independent, so the SEs are too small, the CIs too narrow and the p-values too small: false positives become more likely (recall §6.2.6: the design effect, DEFF). Methods for clustered data are in §15.2.

Normality of residuals protects CIs and p-values in small samples, not the coefficient. It concerns the residuals, not the raw outcome. In large samples linear regression is valid for almost any residual distribution, through the Central Limit Theorem (Lumley et al., 2002).
Equal variance protects the standard errors. If residuals fan out as fitted values grow (heteroscedasticity), a single s is too small in part of the range and too large elsewhere.
Linearity failures corrupt the coefficient; the other three corrupt the uncertainty around it.

questions.prompt: A residual-vs-fitted plot shows residuals fanning out into a cone as fitted values increase. Which assumption is violated, and what does it threaten: the coefficient, or something else?
questions.answer: Equal variance (homoscedasticity) is violated: heteroscedasticity. It threatens the standard errors, and so the CIs and p-values built from them. The coefficient itself can remain a reasonable estimate; its reported precision is what becomes unreliable.

questions.prompt: Why does violating independence raise the risk of a false-positive result, rather than just making the estimate less precise?
questions.answer: Correlated observations (children in the same village, repeated visits by one child) carry less information than the same number of independent ones. The model treats each as fresh information, so it computes an SE that is too small. A too-small SE gives too-narrow CIs and too-small p-values, so a null association is declared significant more often than 5% of the time: the Type I error rate rises.

questions.prompt: The clinic regression (SE of the slope 0.011 kg per month) is refitted on children who were in fact sampled in village clusters, with a design effect of 2.44 for the slope. Roughly what is the correct SE, and what happens to the width of the 95% CI?
questions.answer: DEFF multiplies the variance (recall §6.2.6), so the SE is multiplied by √DEFF = √2.44 = 1.56. Correct SE ≈ 0.011 × 1.56 = 0.017 kg per month. The 95% CI is about 1.56 times as wide: roughly 0.150 ± 2 × 0.017 = 0.116 to 0.184 kg per month instead of 0.129 to 0.171.
